h1: Excise and state permits for spirits in India
title: Excise and State Permits for Spirits | Craft Beer School
desc: The licences, registrations and permits a spirits business in India deals with, explained at process level for corporate teams.
teaser: Every bottle of whisky in India travels with paperwork. Here is what the main licences and permits are and why they shape the business.
standfirst: For people who work in spirits companies but not in the excise team, the permits behind a bottle can look like a black box. This guide explains the main licences, registrations and movement permits at process level, so the dates and delays in your plans make sense.
sections: Why spirits regulation is mostly state level

In India, alcohol for human consumption is kept outside GST. States levy excise duty on it and control its manufacture, movement and sale within their borders. Central rules still apply in some areas, such as food safety standards and packaged goods labelling, but the day-to-day permissions come from each state's excise department.

So the same company deals with a different set of forms, fees and timelines in each state where it makes or sells spirits. Rules and fees vary by state and change, so always work from the current state notification or a licensing consultant. This guide describes the process, not legal advice.
The licences a production site usually needs

A distillery or bottling plant typically operates under several permissions at once:

  • A state licence to manufacture or bottle spirits, issued by the excise department, with conditions on premises, equipment and records.
  • A bonded warehouse licence for holding spirit before duty is paid.
  • A food business licence under the national food safety regulator, which also sets standards for alcoholic beverages.
  • Legal metrology registration for packaged goods, covering declared quantity and label details.
  • Environmental consents from the state pollution control board, important for distilleries because of the volume of effluent they produce.

Other approvals, such as factory and fire safety licences, apply as for any manufacturing site. Our guide on the distillery licence process goes into more detail for new sites.

Spirit production happens under excise supervision. Depending on the state, excise officials may be stationed at the plant or carry out regular checks. Stocks of spirit are recorded in registers at each stage: receipt, production, maturation, blending, bottling and dispatch.

The floor detail that surprises most corporate staff is how closely losses are watched. States set permissible limits for wastage in processes such as maturation, storage and transit. Losses above those limits may need to be explained and can attract duty or penalties. That is why distillery teams measure and record strength and volume so carefully at every transfer.
Brand and label registration happens state by state

Each brand usually has to be registered with the excise department of every state where it will be sold, often pack size by pack size. The label is approved as part of that process. Registrations are commonly renewed for each excise year, which in many states runs from April to March.

The state also needs the price. Producers declare a price, such as an ex-distillery price. The state calculates duty and in many cases fixes or approves the maximum retail price. Our guides to state labelling rules and MRP changes cover those steps.

Spirits move under permit. Bulk spirit sent from a distillery to a bottling plant in another state needs an export permit from the sending state and an import permit from the receiving one. Finished bottles moving from a plant or bonded warehouse to a wholesaler move against transport passes, with quantities and vehicle details recorded.

Many states now handle these permits through online systems, which makes them easier to track but no less strict. A consignment that arrives with paperwork that does not match the load can be held. For planners, permit lead times are as real as manufacturing lead times.
Spirit for drinking and spirit for industry are kept apart

The same distillery equipment can make alcohol for drinks or for industrial use, such as solvents, chemicals and fuel. States treat the two very differently. Spirit meant for human consumption carries excise duty. Spirit for industrial use is often denatured, made undrinkable with additives, so it cannot be diverted into drinks.

For a whisky company that buys extra neutral alcohol from another distillery to blend, every transfer needs its own permit, showing quantity, strength and destination. The supplying distillery and the receiving bottler both record it. The figures must match within the allowed losses. Analysts who see a gap between spirit bought and spirit used should ask about transfer losses and permit timing before assuming a production problem. The paperwork often explains the gap.
Security labels and tracking are spreading

To fight duty evasion and counterfeit liquor, many states require security features on every bottle: holograms, excise adhesive labels or codes that can be scanned through the supply chain. These are often supplied or authorised by the state and must be ordered, accounted for and applied on the line.

For operations teams, this adds a component that cannot be bought on the open market and must be reconciled bottle by bottle. Running short of state security labels stops a bottling line as surely as running short of glass.
A first step: build a permit calendar

Excise work is mostly about dates. Make a single calendar, by state, of licence renewals, brand registration windows, price approval cycles and typical permit lead times. Share it with sales, planning and marketing. Most of the launch delays and stock-outs blamed on excise turn out to be missed dates that were known months earlier.
faqs: Is alcohol covered by GST in India?
Alcohol for human consumption is outside GST. States levy excise duty and set their own rules for its manufacture, movement and sale.
Why does every state need a separate brand registration?
Each state's excise department controls what may be sold within its borders, including the label and the price, so registration happens state by state.
